sentences.text: Venaticosuchus was a medium-sized carnivore belonging to the family Ornithosuchidae, a group of facultatively bipedal crocodylomorphs that thrived during the Late Triassic.
Although it is described as a medium-sized predator reaching up to two meters in length, the total body size remains unknown because fossils preserve only skull and jaw fragments.
The preserved jaw measures 26.0 centimeters in total length and features a toothless gap, known as a diastema, separating the toothed maxilla and premaxilla bones on the snout.
The maxilla contained eight large, serrated teeth with the second tooth being the largest, while the first two teeth of the lower jaw were very large, unserrated, and oval in cross-section.

Distinctive skull features include a cheek bone with a Y-shaped ascending process forming the lower edge of the eye socket and basipterygoid processes separated from the basitubera by a notch forming an acute angle of approximately 60 degrees.

The lower jaw was robust and proportionally more similar to Ornithosuchus than to Riojasuchus, with enlarged front teeth overlapping the snout at the level of the upper jaw gap and an elongated angular bone covered with striations.

The holotype specimen displayed a swollen, rough-textured area of bone on the left side of its skull likely caused by a facial infection, alongside a left upper jaw missing two tooth sockets compared to the right side.
This animal was found in a rock layer dominated by fossils of the rhynchosaur Teyumbaita, suggesting it shared its environment with these herbivorous reptiles.
The genus Venaticosuchus was first described by José Bonaparte in 1971, containing only one known species, Venaticosuchus rusconii, with the holotype specimen cataloged as PVL 2578.
Fossils were discovered at Cerro Las Lajas in La Rioja province, where biostratigraphic evidence suggests the layer dates between 227.94 and 227.24 million years ago.
These remains come from the Late Triassic (Carnian) Ischigualasto Formation deposited approximately 230 million years ago, and the original description was published in 1970 or 1971.

Reconstructions indicate Venaticosuchus possessed a slow but powerful bite force, supported by the highest combined adductor muscle moment arm value of any ornithosuchid, meaning its jaw muscles took a long time to retract.
This slow but strong bite contrasts with the fast bites of modern crocodilians and basal aetosaurs, sharing this trait with other ornithosuchids and the aetosaur Desmatosuchus.
Venaticosuchus is believed to have been a specialized scavenger rather than a predator of live prey.
The generic name Venaticosuchus combines the Latin word for hunting and the Greek word for crocodile, a name coined by Bonaparte in 1971.
Venaticosuchus was originally thought to be an ancestor of large theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus, but is now known to be more closely related to crocodilians.
The only known species, Venaticosuchus rusconii, lived in Argentina during the Late Triassic, with a time range estimated from 233.6 to 227.3 million years ago during the Carnian stage.

While one hypothesis suggests Venaticosuchus was a specialized scavenger that used its strong bite to process carcasses, a 2023 study suggests it may have been piscivorous, capturing small aquatic animals underwater and swallowing them whole, similar to a heron or Spinosaurus.
